newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore dollar gains on finance minister comment.
newsitem.headline: Singapore dollar gains on finance minister comment.

text.p: The Singapore dollar gained sharply on Monday as players liquidated long U.S. dollar and ringgit positions following comments by Singapore's Finance Minister Richard Hu at the weekend.

Dealers said the U.S. dollar was sold down from its opening S$1.4450/55 on Hu's remark that the Singapore dollar could be expected to maintain its more modest rise of recent years if the global inflationary environment remained favourable.
"To the extent that foreign inflationary pressures become more muted, our exchange rate does not have to appreciate as much as it did before," Hu said.

He also repeated Singapore's policy objective of maintaining a strong currency to shield against foreign inflationary pressures in an economy where 60 cents out of every dollar spent is on imported goods.

Late afternoon sales of the U.S. dollar and Malaysian ringgit by European players pushed dollar/Sing below the psychologically important S$1.4400 level while the ringgit/Sing cross fell through 58 Singapore cents.
The U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.4376/86 and the ringgit at 57.94/58.00 Singapore cents after the Asian close.
"The market is still caught long in the dollar/Sing and ringgit/Sing. Once the dollar hit the stops below 1.4400, there was a lot of selling off from there," said a U.S. bank dealer.
He said there was some buying interest from U.S. funds around the 1.4355/60 level in dollar/Sing and at 57.90 in ringgit/Sing.
"For the time being, I think 1.4350/60 should see some very good support," he said, adding, however, that the market would have trouble breaching its longer-term target of 1.4500.
Alison Seng, analyst at MMS Standard and Poor's, said Hu's comments reminded people that Singapore's policy of allowing a gradual appreciation of its currency was unchanged.
Seng said dollar/Sing and ringgit/Sing had been bought excessively last week and players took the comments as a "signal for the market to cool down a bit".

A joint statement by the governments of Brunei and Singapore categorically denying rumours they were contemplating ending their currency interchangeability agreement also fuelled buying of the Singapore dollar, dealers said.

Speculation that Brunei might end its currency peg with the Singapore dollar surfaced late last month amid talk the oil kingdom might withdraw from the agreement in an effort to make its non-oil exports more competitive.
"We're currently seeing some support (for the U.S. dollar) at 1.4350/60. But 1.4300/20 is a more important base. If that's broken, we see a major reversal," Seng said.
Research firm I.D.E.A. said in a daily commentary that the Sing dollar had already set a slower trend of appreciation.

"Considering that the Sing dollar's uptrend will be maintained, current Sing dollar levels are too weak. From 1.4000 at end 1996, the Sing dollar is likely to end the year around 1.4000/4100, which means that dollar/Sing remains a sell at current levels," it said.
